title: How the World Was Made
subtitle: A creation narrative in Mooney's field collection

learningObjectives.text: What brings up the mud that becomes land?

earth.author: James Mooney
earth.locator: Myth 1 · HOW THE WORLD WAS MADE, normalized characters 26-932
earth.excerpt: The earth is a great island floating in a sea of water, and suspended at each of the four cardinal points by a cord hanging down from the sky vault, which is of solid rock. When the world grows old and worn out, the people will die and the cords will break and let the earth sink down into the ocean, and all will be water again. The Indians are afraid of this. When all was water, the animals were above in Galûñ'lati, beyond the arch; but it was very much crowded, and they were wanting more room. They wondered what was below the water, and at last Dâyuni'si, "Beaver's Grandchild," the little Water-beetle, offered to go and see if it could learn. It darted in every direction over the surface of the water, but could find no firm place to rest. Then it dived to the bottom and came up with some soft mud, which began to grow and spread on every side until it became the island which we call the earth.
earth.note: Verbatim English text from Mooney's 1902 collection. Keep the specific numbered story and its East Cherokee/recorded-source context attached.

buzzard.author: James Mooney
buzzard.locator: Myth 1 · HOW THE WORLD WAS MADE, normalized characters 1487-1882
buzzard.excerpt: When he reached the Cherokee country, he was very tired, and his wings began to flap and strike the ground, and wherever they struck the earth there was a valley, and where they turned up again there was a mountain. When the animals above saw this, they were afraid that the whole world would be mountains, so they called him back, but the Cherokee country remains full of mountains to this day.

narrativeBlocks.title: Land begins in water
narrativeBlocks.body: Mooney's recorded narrative describes the earth as an island above water. The Water-beetle dives to the bottom and brings up soft mud.

narrativeBlocks.title: A bird shapes the land
narrativeBlocks.body: Quotation from Mooney's English record (whitespace normalized): “When he reached the Cherokee country, he was very tired, and his wings began to flap and strike the ground, and wherever they struck the earth there was a valley, and where they turned up again there was a mountain. When the animals above saw this, they were afraid that the whole world would be mountains, so they called him back, but the Cherokee country remains full of mountains to this day.”

narrativeBlocks.title: A Cherokee place enters the story
narrativeBlocks.body: The Great Buzzard's wings strike the soft earth; Mooney's version connects those impacts with valleys and mountains in Cherokee country.

narrativeBlocks.title: Scope the record
narrativeBlocks.body: Mooney collected this work chiefly among Eastern Cherokee communities in North Carolina, with some additional material from western communities. It is not every Cherokee creation account.

narrativeBlocks.title: Keep the story version visible
narrativeBlocks.body: The earth-making and mountain-making details here are from Mooney's printed English record; later readers should not silently merge other Cherokee versions.
